levels.title: Cut and Paste
levels.concept: Excision and good pairs; H̃(X/A); homology of spheres.

design.site: Excision Cut — the delta's far bank, a quarry where pieces of land can be cut out and collapsed.
design.story: Cut out a piece well inside a part and the relative count doesn't change. Collapse a part to a point (0-5) and the relative count becomes ordinary homology. With these, Gyroid finally computes the homology of spheres: a sphere has a hole in exactly one dimension.
design.objective: Excise and collapse to compute homology, and find the hole in every sphere.
mechanics: Excision saw: cut a region whose closure sits inside the interior of A; the relative meter stays the same.
Collapse press (0-5 Cone Zone): squash A to a point; for a good pair the relative homology equals the reduced homology of X/A.
Sphere ladder: Dⁿ with its rim collapsed is Sⁿ; climb the ladder using the pair sequence one dimension at a time.
design.math_check: Excision; good pairs and H̃(X/A) ≅ H(X, A); H̃ₖ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ for k = n and 0 otherwise; Sᵐ ≇ Sⁿ, ℝᵐ ≇ ℝⁿ for m ≠ n; no retraction Dⁿ → Sⁿ⁻¹ (Hatcher pp. 118–128).

stages.name: Cut Deep
stages.description: Excise a region inside A; the relative meter doesn't flinch.

stages.name: Collapse
stages.description: Squash a disk's rim to a point: a sphere appears on the press.

stages.name: The Ladder
stages.description: Climb from S¹ to S³, carrying the single hole up one dimension each rung.

stages.name: Too Close to the Edge
stages.description: Null's saw cuts a region touching A's edge; show why excision fails there, then fix the cut.

enemies.name: Coner
enemies.description: From 0-5: caps holes with cones.

enemies.name: Quarry golem
enemies.description: New: a violet stone hulk that welds excised pieces back; three lashes.

design.tools: Uses the Boundary Blade, Suspension Sling and Collapse press.
design.music: Chain Delta theme with quarry percussion (stone clacks) and a rising figure on each rung of the ladder.
design.visuals: A stone quarry on the far bank; glowing gold saw cuts; a press squashing a disk's rim into a point to form a sphere; a ladder of nested spheres.

art.scene: Level 'Cut and Paste' at the Excision Cut: a stone quarry on a river bank; glowing gold saw cuts in the rock; a great press squashing the rim of a stone disk into a single point so it bulges into a sphere; a ladder of nested glowing spheres climbing up. Gyroid operates the press. A violet stone golem lurks.

levels.title: The Third Degree
levels.concept: Degree of sphere maps; antipodal map; hairy ball theorem.
levels.goal: Refute Null's World-1 claim: H₂(S²) ≅ ℤ sees the hollow that loops missed.

design.site: Dynamo Gate — the base of the Degree Dynamo, where great brass spheres turn on axles and wrap around each other.
design.story: Null's sphere claimed loops were blind to its hollow. Homology isn't: H₂ of the sphere is ℤ. Each dynamo maps a sphere onto a sphere; its degree counts how many times. The antipodal dynamo flips orientation in odd dimensions, and no wind can blow over a sphere without a calm spot.
design.objective: Refute Null's World 1 claim, measure degrees of sphere maps, and comb the hairy ball.
mechanics: Degree Dial (new): set on a dynamo, it shows how many times the source sphere wraps its target (via H_n).
Reflections have degree −1; compositions multiply degrees; maps that slide into each other have equal degree.
Antipodal dynamo: degree (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ on Sⁿ.
Wind comb: try to set wind arrows on every tile of a sphere island with no calm spot; on S² it can't be done.
design.math_check: H₂(S²) ≅ ℤ (refutes the World 1 claim that S² has no hole); degree of maps Sⁿ → Sⁿ, properties, antipodal map has degree (−1)ⁿ⁺¹; Sⁿ has a nowhere-zero tangent vector field iff n is odd (Hatcher pp. 134–137).

stages.name: The Hollow, Seen
stages.description: Measure Null's sphere: H₂ = ℤ. The hollow is real.

stages.name: Wrap Count
stages.description: Set dynamos to wrap a sphere 0, 1, 2 and −1 times.

stages.name: Through the Center
stages.description: The antipodal dynamo on circle and sphere: degree +1 on S¹, −1 on S².

stages.name: The Hairy Ball
stages.description: Comb the sphere island: one calm spot always remains. Then comb the circle smoothly.

enemies.name: Winder
enemies.description: From 1-3: now wraps spheres, not just circles.

enemies.name: Gale spawn
enemies.description: New: violet wisps that blow wind across tiles; lash to calm them.

design.tools: Unlocks the Degree Dial (degree_dial).
design.music: Degree Dynamo theme: an industrial 110 bpm march in A minor, brass stabs on each full wrap, a low turbine hum.
design.visuals: Great brass spheres turning on axles, one wrapping a translucent skin around another, gold lightning arcing between them; a sphere island with arrows swirling around a single calm spot.

art.scene: Level 'The Third Degree' at the Degree Dynamo: great brass spheres turning on axles, one wrapping a translucent skin twice around another, gold lightning arcing between them. In the foreground a small sphere island covered in glowing wind arrows swirling around a single calm spot. Gyroid holds a glowing dial. Count Null's pale sphere visible far away.

levels.title: Cell Block
levels.concept: Cellular homology from a CW structure; Euler characteristic revisited.

design.site: Cell Block — a fortress-workshop where places are built cell by cell (0-4) and their homology read off the cells.
design.story: With a cell structure, homology needs only the cells: one group per dimension, joined by maps whose entries are degrees. Torus, projective plane and Klein bottle reveal their holes in a few lines, and the Euler characteristic from the Timber Yard returns as the alternating count of holes.
design.objective: Compute homology from cells and degrees, and check χ against the holes.
mechanics: Cell chain: each dimension's cells are a stack of crates; the attaching maps' degrees (Degree Dial) become arrows between stacks.
Read holes: kernel over image at each stack, as in 2-2.
Torsion: on RP² the 1-cell's boundary runs around twice: H₁ = ℤ₂ — a loop that dies when doubled (1-7).
χ check: alternating sum of cells equals alternating sum of hole ranks.
design.math_check: Cellular homology, the cellular boundary formula via degrees, homology of the torus, RP², Klein bottle and CPⁿ; χ = Σ(−1)ⁿ rank Hₙ (Hatcher pp. 137–149).

stages.name: Crates
stages.description: A sphere as one 0-cell and one 2-cell: holes in dimension 0 and 2.

stages.name: The Torus
stages.description: All boundary degrees zero: ℤ, ℤ², ℤ.

stages.name: The Doubled Edge
stages.description: RP²: the 2-cell wraps the edge twice: torsion ℤ₂ appears.

stages.name: Census
stages.description: Verify χ for five places both ways.

enemies.name: Unglue
enemies.description: From 0-4.

enemies.name: Loop-biter
enemies.description: From 0-6.

design.visuals: A stone fortress-workshop with stacked glowing crates by dimension, gold arrows between stacks, a projective plane forming from a disk with its rim doubled.

art.scene: Level 'Cell Block': a stone fortress-workshop with glowing crates stacked in three columns, gold arrows between the columns; in the center a disk whose rim is being wrapped around twice to form a projective plane. Gyroid works with a brass-and-indigo gauntlet.

levels.title: Patchwork
levels.concept: Mayer–Vietoris sequences.

design.site: Patchwork Fields — fields covered by overlapping canvas patches.
design.story: Cover a place with two overlapping patches. Their holes and the overlap's holes link in a long exact sequence: Mayer–Vietoris. It is the homology version of Van Kampen (1-7).
design.objective: Compute homology from two overlapping patches.
mechanics: Lay patches A and B over a place so their interiors cover it.
The Mayer–Vietoris locks: overlap → A ⊕ B → whole → (one dimension down) overlap…
Chase through it as in 2-4.
design.math_check: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence; homology of Sⁿ by hemispheres; of the torus and Klein bottle by annuli (Hatcher pp. 149–153).

stages.name: Two Hemispheres
stages.description: Cover a sphere by two caps overlapping in a band.

stages.name: Two Annuli
stages.description: Cover the torus by two cylinders.

stages.name: The Twisted Patch
stages.description: Same for the Klein bottle: a twist in the overlap changes the answer.

stages.name: Patch It Yourself
stages.description: Choose your own cover for a new place.

enemies.name: Unglue
enemies.description: Pulls patches apart.

enemies.name: Leak sprite
enemies.description: Breaks exactness.

design.music: Degree Dynamo theme as a folk reel — fiddle-like square wave.
design.visuals: Rolling fields under great overlapping canvas patches, glowing gold seams where they overlap.

art.scene: Level 'Patchwork' in Patchwork Fields: rolling fields under two great overlapping canvas patches held up on poles, glowing gold seams where they overlap; under them, a torus-shaped hill. Gyroid clips two patches together with a copper clasp.

levels.title: Mod Squad
levels.concept: Homology with coefficients; ℤ₂ and nonorientable surfaces.

design.site: Mod Mill — a waterwheel mill that grinds counts down mod 2.
design.story: Count holes with even-or-odd instead of whole numbers and some surfaces suddenly speak up: a Klein bottle or projective plane, invisible to ℤ in the top dimension, has a top hole mod 2. Arrows stop mattering.
design.objective: Compute homology with coefficients and detect non-orientable surfaces.
mechanics: The mill's wheel switches the meter's coefficients between ℤ and ℤ₂ (and ℤₙ).
Mod 2, edge directions don't matter: flipped arrows count the same.
Non-orientable test: H₂ with ℤ₂ is ℤ₂ while H₂ with ℤ is 0.
design.math_check: Homology with coefficients; Hₙ(M; ℤ₂) ≅ ℤ₂ for closed connected n-manifolds; Hₙ(M; ℤ) = 0 for non-orientable ones (Hatcher pp. 153–160).

stages.name: Even or Odd
stages.description: Recount the torus mod 2.

stages.name: The Projective Plane
stages.description: H₂ mod 2 lights; H₂ with ℤ doesn't.

stages.name: Flippers Lose
stages.description: Mod 2, Flipper frogs can't disrupt anything.

stages.name: Sort the Surfaces
stages.description: Sort surfaces into orientable and not.

enemies.name: Flipper
enemies.description: Harmless mod 2 — a comic beat.

enemies.name: Bog spawn
enemies.description: Hides holes.

levels.title: Forget the Order
levels.concept: H₁ is π₁ made abelian; the Commutator's trick vanishes in homology.

design.site: Abelian Ford — a shallow ford where the Commutator's ribbon patrols try to cross into the delta.
design.story: The Commutator follows Gyroid into the delta. But here H₁ is the abelianization of π₁: order is forgotten, and his word a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ counts as nothing. His patrols can't pass.
design.objective: Use homology to dissolve the Commutator's patrol words.
mechanics: Ford meter: a patrol's word becomes a vector of letter totals (a counts minus a⁻¹ counts, and the same for b).
Commutators total zero: they are boundaries in the ford.
Patrols whose word totals zero dissolve when they enter the ford; others must be lashed.
design.math_check: H₁(X) ≅ π₁(X)ᵃᵇ for path-connected X; commutators map to zero (Hatcher pp. 166–168).

stages.name: Totals
stages.description: Read patrol words as totals.

stages.name: Dissolve
stages.description: Lure commutator patrols into the ford.

stages.name: Not Everything Dies
stages.description: A patrol walking a a b survives: its totals are (2, 1).

stages.name: Hold the Ford
stages.description: Defend the ford against a mixed wave.

enemies.name: Ribbon patrol
enemies.description: From World 1: dissolves in the ford if its totals are zero.

enemies.name: The Commutator (cameo)
enemies.description: Watches from the far bank and withdraws.

levels.title: Classic Moves
levels.concept: Bonus: Jordan curve theorem, invariance of domain, division algebras.

design.site: Jordan Ring — an island ringed by a single closed wall.
design.story: Classic results with Gyroid's new tools: any closed wall in the plane splits it into an inside and an outside; open sets of the same dimension can't be squeezed into different shapes; and only a few dimensions allow division.
design.objective: Prove the wall has an inside, using homology.
mechanics: Draw any closed wall (no self-crossing) with the Spool; the meter reports two regions.
Invariance of domain demo: a squeezed open patch remains open.
design.math_check: Jordan curve theorem (via Sⁿ minus an embedded sphere), invariance of domain, a commutative division algebra structure on ℝⁿ exists only for n = 1, 2 (Hatcher pp. 169–177). Flag: the full 1, 2, 4, 8 theorem needs K-theory beyond Ch. 2; the game only mentions it.

stages.name: Draw a Wall
stages.description: Any wall: two sides.

stages.description: Even a wildly wiggly wall splits the plane in two.

enemies.description: Puzzle bonus.

levels.title: Fixed Ideas
levels.concept: Bonus: simplicial approximation and the Lefschetz fixed point theorem.

design.site: Lefschetz Lantern — a lighthouse whose beam maps the island onto itself.
design.story: The lantern's beam maps a place to itself. Add up the traces of the induced maps on homology: if the total isn't zero, some point maps to itself — a generalization of Brouwer (1-4).
design.objective: Compute Lefschetz numbers and find fixed points.
mechanics: Lantern beam: a map f of the island to itself, shown as arrows.
Trace tally: the tally sums traces of f_* with alternating signs.
Nonzero tally guarantees a lit fixed point; zero tally allows a fixed-point-free map (e.g., rotating a circle).
design.math_check: Simplicial approximation; the Lefschetz fixed point theorem for finite simplicial complexes or their retracts (Hatcher pp. 177–184).

stages.name: Trace
stages.description: Rotate a circle: tally zero, no fixed point needed.

stages.name: Always a Fixed Point
stages.description: Any map of a disk or projective plane has tally 1: find the point.

enemies.name: None
enemies.description: Puzzle bonus.

art.scene: Bonus level 'Fixed Ideas' at the Lefschetz Lantern: a stone lighthouse on a rocky point at night, its gold beam sweeping across an island covered with gold arrows, one arrow-free glowing spot where the beam rests. Gyroid at the lighthouse door.

castle.title: The Retractor
castle.outcome: Null's ball-to-boundary retractor B³ → S² is impossible because H₂(B³) = 0 — Brouwer again, one dimension up.

design.site: The Retractor — Null's dome built around a hollow stone ball; his engine tries to squash the solid ball onto its surface.
design.story: Null rebuilds his Retractor, one dimension up: crush the whole ball onto its skin. If it worked, the sphere's hole would come from a ball that has none. Gyroid proves it can't work, and Null flees to the gardens.
design.objective: Wreck the ball-to-sphere Retractor.

phases.name: The ball
phases.description: Null's engine squeezes the ball's interior toward its skin. Measure: H₂ of the ball is 0, H₂ of the sphere is ℤ. Tests 2-5.

phases.name: The skin
phases.description: Null's sphere-shields spin; set the Degree Dial to match and reverse each shield's degree to break it. Tests 2-6.

phases.name: The cells
phases.description: Null rebuilds the ball from cells to hide a hole; compute cellular homology to expose that it has none. Tests 2-7.

phases.name: Seize
phases.description: The engine would turn the sphere's hole into nothing and back: it seizes. Null escapes.

enemies.description: Boss (escapes).

enemies.description: From 1-4, now 3D.

design.movie: castle-2-intro “The Retractor, Again” and castle-2-outro “Classes Multiply”.

worlds.title: Cup Product Gardens
worlds.theme: Signal gardens where cochains read chains backwards and classes multiply.

null_claim.claim: Every map S³ → S² is trivial — homology sees nothing there.
null_claim.why_it_works_here: H̃_*(S³) and H̃_*(S²) live in different degrees, so homology gives no map to detect.

levels.title: Reverse Engineering
levels.concept: Cochains and coboundaries: dualize chains into a coefficient group G.

design.site: Mirror Pools — still pools that reflect every garden path backwards.
design.story: In the Gardens, the gardeners don't walk paths — they read them. A cochain is a reading: it assigns a value to every edge (or triangle). Its coboundary reads a triangle by reading its edges. The mirror pools show the delta's chains reversed: what was a boundary is now a coboundary.
design.objective: Assign readings to edges and triangles and compute coboundaries.
mechanics: Reading wand: set a value from a coefficient group G on every edge of a garden patch (a 1-cochain).
Coboundary: the pool shows the reading of each triangle as the signed sum of its edges' readings (δφ = φ∘∂).
δδ = 0 again, mirrored from 2-2.
Cocycles (δφ = 0) modulo coboundaries give cohomology classes.
design.math_check: Cochains Cⁿ(X; G) = Hom(Cₙ(X), G), δ dual to ∂, δδ = 0, Hⁿ(X; G) = ker δ / im δ (Hatcher pp. 190–197).

stages.name: Read an Edge
stages.description: Give each edge a value; the pool reads triangles from their edges.

stages.name: Balanced Readings
stages.description: Find readings with every triangle reading zero: cocycles.

stages.name: Readings from Points
stages.description: Readings that come from vertex values (differences) are coboundaries — they don't count.

stages.name: Around the Hole
stages.description: On an annulus, find a cocycle that isn't a coboundary: it reads 1 around the hole.

enemies.name: Echo
enemies.description: New: a violet reflection that mirrors Gyroid's moves with signs flipped; lash it in the pool, not on land.

enemies.name: Flipper
enemies.description: From 2-1.

design.music: Cup Product Gardens theme: a gentle 76 bpm waltz in F major, celesta and soft strings — first statement, with the melody sometimes played retrograde.
design.visuals: Twilight gardens of stone paths with still mirror pools reflecting them; gold values glowing on edges; reflected arrows pointing the opposite way.

art.scene: Level 'Reverse Engineering' at the Mirror Pools: twilight gardens with blue-gray stone paths and still mirror pools that reflect the paths; glowing gold values hover over path edges, and their reflections in the pools show arrows pointing the opposite way. Gyroid holds a slim gold wand. A violet reflection of a figure moves inside a pool.

levels.title: Torsion Shift
levels.concept: Universal Coefficient Theorem: torsion appears one degree higher; cohomology of spaces.

design.site: Torsion Terrace — a terrace where twisted vines climb from one level to the next.
design.story: Cohomology is determined by homology — but torsion climbs up one floor. The projective plane's twisted loop (2-7) shows up in cohomology one dimension higher.
design.objective: Predict cohomology from homology using the Universal Coefficient rule.
mechanics: Terrace levels hold homology groups from Chain Delta.
Free parts stay on their own terrace; torsion vines climb to the next terrace (Ext).
Coefficient switch: with ℤ₂ readings the vines behave differently.
design.math_check: The universal coefficient theorem Hⁿ(X; G) ≅ Hom(Hₙ(X), G) ⊕ Ext(Hₙ₋₁(X), G); cohomology of RP², lens spaces (Hatcher pp. 190–206).

stages.name: Free Floors
stages.description: Torus: cohomology matches homology terrace for terrace.

stages.name: The Climbing Vine
stages.description: RP²: H₁ = ℤ₂ climbs to H² = ℤ₂.

stages.name: Change the Soil
stages.description: With ℤ₂ coefficients RP² reads ℤ₂ on every terrace.

stages.name: Plan the Terrace
stages.description: Predict cohomology for a lens space before reading it.

enemies.name: Vine choker
enemies.description: New: a violet vine that pulls torsion back down; two lashes.

design.tools: Uses the reading wand and the Mod Mill switch (2-9).
design.music: Gardens theme with a rising sequence each time a vine climbs.
design.visuals: Stacked stone terraces with twisted glowing gold vines climbing from each level to the next.

art.scene: Level 'Torsion Shift' at the Torsion Terrace: stacked stone garden terraces at twilight; twisted glowing gold vines climb from each terrace up to the next. Gyroid climbs beside a vine. A violet vine strangles one.

levels.title: Front Face, Back Face
levels.concept: Cup product on simplices and the coboundary sign rule.

design.site: Lantern Rows — rows of lantern posts, each lantern lit by a reading.
design.story: Two readings can multiply: read a triangle's front edge with one and its back edge with the other. Gyroid forges the Cup Caster, which pours two lanterns into one — and swapping their order may flip the sign.
design.objective: Multiply cochains with the Cup Caster and learn the sign rule.
mechanics: Cup Caster (new): pick two lit lanterns (cochains φ, ψ); on each triangle, the product reads φ on the front face and ψ on the back face.
Coboundary rule: δ(φ ⌣ ψ) = δφ ⌣ ψ ± φ ⌣ δψ — products of cocycles are cocycles; products with coboundaries are coboundaries.
Graded commutativity: swapping two degree-1 lanterns flips the sign.
design.math_check: The cup product on simplicial/singular cochains, the coboundary formula, the induced product on cohomology, graded commutativity αβ = (−1)ᵏˡ βα (Hatcher pp. 206–212; graded commutativity p. 215).

stages.name: Front and Back
stages.description: Cup two edge readings on a single triangle.

stages.name: Products of Cocycles
stages.description: Cup two cocycles: the product is a cocycle.

stages.name: Swap
stages.description: Swap the order of two degree-1 lanterns: the light inverts.

stages.name: Light the Row
stages.description: Light a target lantern on a torus as a product of two.

enemies.description: Flips signs.

enemies.name: Moth swarm
enemies.description: New: violet moths that put lanterns out; one lash each.

levels.title: A Cup of Counterexample
levels.concept: The cohomology ring distinguishes the torus from S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S².
levels.goal: Refute Null's World-2 claim with a nonzero cup product.

design.site: Twin Islands — Null's two islands from the end of World 2, the torus and the two-loops-plus-sphere, side by side.
design.story: Null's World 2 claim: the torus and S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S² are the same place — their holes match. The Cup Caster tells them apart: on the torus, the two loop readings multiply to the top class. On the bouquet, their product is zero.
design.objective: Refute Null's World 2 claim with a nonzero cup product.
mechanics: Light the two degree-1 lanterns on each island.
Cup them: on the torus the top lantern lights; on the bouquet it stays dark.
Since cup products are preserved by homotopy equivalence, the islands aren't the same place.
design.math_check: Cohomology rings of T² and S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S²: same groups, different products; the ring is a homotopy invariant (Hatcher pp. 212–214). Refutes the World 2 claim.

levels.title: Product Placement
levels.concept: Künneth formula for products.

design.site: Product Parterre — a formal garden laid out as a grid, each bed the product of a row and a column.
design.story: The cohomology of a product is built from its factors: rows times columns. The torus is a circle times a circle (1-5), and its lanterns are products of the circles' lanterns.
design.objective: Compute product cohomology from factors.
mechanics: Row and column beds hold each factor's lanterns; a bed lights with their cross product.
Künneth: for nice coefficients, the product's lanterns are exactly the bed products.
design.math_check: Cross product and the Künneth formula H*(X × Y; R) ≅ H*(X; R) ⊗ H*(Y; R) for H*(Y; R) free and finitely generated (Hatcher pp. 214–220).

levels.title: Polynomial Garden
levels.concept: RPⁿ and CPⁿ have truncated polynomial cohomology; Borsuk–Ulam.

design.site: Polynomial Garden — a garden of nested lantern rings: one lantern, its square, its cube, until the top.
design.story: On projective spaces, one lantern generates everything: its powers light the whole garden until they reach the top. With this, Borsuk–Ulam returns in every dimension.
design.objective: Compute truncated polynomial rings and prove Borsuk–Ulam.
mechanics: Power steps: cup a lantern with itself repeatedly; each power lights the next ring.
RPⁿ with ℤ₂: the powers of α light rings 0..n; αⁿ⁺¹ = 0. CPⁿ with ℤ: powers of a degree-2 class.
Borsuk–Ulam: a map commuting with antipodes would force αⁿ⁺¹ ≠ 0 in a smaller garden — impossible.
design.math_check: H*(RPⁿ; ℤ₂) ≅ ℤ₂[α]/(αⁿ⁺¹), H*(CPⁿ; ℤ) ≅ ℤ[α]/(αⁿ⁺¹); Borsuk–Ulam (Hatcher pp. 220–229).

stages.description: On RP², α ⌣ α lights the top.

levels.title: Which Way Is Up
levels.concept: Orientations; local homology; the orientation double cover.

design.site: Compass Cliffs — sea cliffs on Poincaré Reach where small compasses spin at every point.
design.story: A place is orientable if compasses can be set consistently everywhere. Every place has an orientation double cover — two sheets, one for each choice (1-8) — and it is connected exactly when the place can't be oriented.
design.objective: Set local orientations and build the orientation double cover.
mechanics: Local compass: at each point, choose one of two orientations (a local homology generator).
Carry the compass along paths; returning flipped means non-orientable.
Sheet Compass: the two choices make a two-sheet cover; on a Möbius cliff it is one connected strip.
design.math_check: Local homology Hₙ(M, M − x) ≅ ℤ, orientations, the orientation double cover (Hatcher pp. 233–239).

levels.title: Both Sides of the Story
levels.concept: Poincaré duality: Hᵏ ≅ Hₙ₋ₖ for closed orientable manifolds; ℤ₂ otherwise.

design.site: The Seam — a glowing seam down Poincaré Reach where the land mirrors itself; every tower on one side has a twin on the other.
design.story: On a closed oriented manifold, holes in dimension k match readings in dimension n − k. Every tower has a twin across the seam. Without orientation, the match still works mod 2.
design.objective: Pair holes with readings across the seam (Poincaré duality).
mechanics: Dual cells: each k-cell has a dual (n−k)-cell crossing it once.
Seam mirror: holes on one side light their dual readings on the other.
Non-orientable: switch to ℤ₂ readings to restore the mirror.
design.math_check: Poincaré duality Hᵏ(M; ℤ) ≅ Hₙ₋ₖ(M; ℤ) for closed orientable n-manifolds; with ℤ₂ for all closed manifolds; dual cell decompositions as intuition (Hatcher pp. 239–249).

levels.title: Perfect Pairing
levels.concept: Duality and cup product: the nondegenerate pairing (CP² vs. S² ∨ S⁴).

design.site: Pairing Pier — a pier where lanterns from opposite sides are paired across the water.
design.story: Duality and cup products together: every lantern has a partner whose product is the top lantern. CP² and S² ∨ S⁴ have the same holes, but only CP²'s middle lantern squares to the top.
design.objective: Use the cup pairing to tell CP² from S² ∨ S⁴.
mechanics: Pair lanterns across the pier; the pairing is perfect (nondegenerate) on a closed orientable manifold.
Square the middle lantern: on CP² it lights the top; on S² ∨ S⁴ it's dark — and S² ∨ S⁴ is not a manifold.
design.math_check: The cup product pairing is nondegenerate mod torsion for closed orientable manifolds; H*(CP²) vs H*(S² ∨ S⁴) (Hatcher pp. 249–252).

castle.title: The Counterfeit Station

worlds.title: Postnikov Spire
worlds.theme: A tower whose rooms unfold into higher dimensions; the Null Crown sits at the top.

null_claim.claim: Give me the homotopy groups and I'll rebuild any space — the twists don't matter.
null_claim.why_it_works_here: Homotopy groups alone don't determine homotopy type; the k-invariants do the gluing.

levels.title: Cube Root
levels.concept: πₙ as cubes with boundary at the basepoint; πₙ is abelian for n ≥ 2 (slide subcubes past each other).

design.site: Cube Hall — the Spire's first floor: a hall of cubes whose faces all fold onto one point.
design.story: Loops were maps of an interval with both ends at the beacon. Now: maps of a cube with its whole surface at the beacon. These are the higher homotopy groups. In two or more dimensions, there's room to slide one cube past another — so order no longer matters.
design.objective: Combine cube-maps and show that higher homotopy groups are abelian.
mechanics: Cube maps: an n-cube whose entire boundary is pinned to the basepoint (an element of πₙ).
Stack: glue two cubes side by side along one direction (the group operation).
Slide: shrink each into a small subcube, slide them around each other in the second direction, and regrow — f + g slides into g + f.
Contrast: in one dimension (World 1) there's no room to pass, which is why the Commutator's word mattered.
design.math_check: πₙ(X, x₀) as homotopy classes of maps (Iⁿ, ∂Iⁿ) → (X, x₀); πₙ is abelian for n ≥ 2 (Hatcher pp. 339–346).

stages.name: Pinned Cubes
stages.description: A square with its whole edge at the beacon is a map of a sphere.

stages.name: Stack
stages.description: Stack squares left-to-right; undo with a reversed square.

stages.description: Shrink, slide past, regrow: order doesn't matter in two dimensions.

stages.description: Try the same slide on intervals and fail — revisit the Commutator's patrol.

levels.title: Snap to Grid
levels.concept: Cellular approximation: πᵢ(Sⁿ) = 0 for i < n; CW approximation.

design.site: Grid Gallery — a gallery where everything snaps to its cell grid.
design.story: Any map between cell-built places can be slid to respect the cells: the k-dimensional part lands in the k-dimensional skeleton. So small spheres can't wrap big ones: πᵢ(Sⁿ) = 0 for i < n.
design.objective: Snap maps to cells and show small spheres slip off big spheres.
mechanics: Snap: slide a map so each k-cell lands in the k-skeleton.
Sphere test: a circle on a 2-sphere snaps into the 0-skeleton — a point — so it shrinks.
CW approximation: replace a strange place by a cell-built one with the same homotopy groups.
design.math_check: Cellular approximation theorem; πᵢ(Sⁿ) = 0 for i < n; CW approximation (Hatcher pp. 348–356).

stages.description: Snap a path to a graph's edges.

levels.title: Weak Spot
levels.concept: Whitehead's theorem: weak equivalences of CW complexes are homotopy equivalences.

design.site: The Weak Spot — a floor where two rooms agree on every homotopy group.
design.story: If a map between cell-built places matches all homotopy groups, it is a full equivalence (0-3 Mirror Couriers return). But beware: matching groups abstractly isn't enough — the map must induce them.
design.objective: Use Whitehead's theorem — and learn what it does not say.
mechanics: Equivalence test: a map that induces isomorphisms on every πₙ between CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence — the Mirror Couriers can be built.
Fake twins: two places with isomorphic groups but no map inducing them (S² × RP³ vs RP² × S³) — not covered by the theorem.
design.math_check: Whitehead's theorem; the need for a map inducing the isomorphisms (Hatcher pp. 346–348, example p. 348).

levels.title: Suspension of Disbelief
levels.concept: Homotopy excision and Freudenthal suspension; πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ via degree.

design.site: Sling Landing — a balcony at the top of the Ascent, open to a vertical shaft.
design.story: Suspending (0-5) shifts homotopy groups up one dimension, and in a range it changes nothing (Freudenthal). The Sling gets its upgrade: lift a whole map up a dimension. And πₙ(Sⁿ) is ℤ, counted by degree (2-6).
design.objective: Suspend maps up the shaft and compute πₙ(Sⁿ).
mechanics: Freudenthal Sling (upgrade of the 0-5 Suspension Sling): suspend a map of spheres; it climbs the shaft.
Stable range: πᵢ(Sⁿ) → πᵢ₊₁(Sⁿ⁺¹) is an isomorphism for i < 2n − 1 and onto for i = 2n − 1.
Degree Dial: maps Sⁿ → Sⁿ are classified by degree.
design.math_check: Homotopy excision, the Freudenthal suspension theorem, πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ via degree (Hatcher pp. 360–366).

levels.title: One Group Per Floor
levels.concept: Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(G, n).

design.site: One-Group Floors — floors with exactly one nonzero homotopy group each.
design.story: The One-Group Tower from World 1 had loops only. These floors generalize it: one group, in one dimension n — the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(G, n), the building blocks of the Spire.
design.objective: Build K(G, n) floors by attaching cells to kill higher groups.
mechanics: Start with a bouquet of n-spheres; attach (n+1)-cells for relations.
Kill: attach higher cells to fill every higher group, floor by floor.

levels.title: Hurewicz Hurrah
levels.concept: Hurewicz theorem: the first nonzero πₙ equals Hₙ.

design.site: Hurewicz Hall — a hall where homotopy and homology meters stand side by side.
design.story: The first nonzero homotopy group equals the first nonzero homology group (World 2) — and in dimension one, homology is π₁ made abelian (2-10).
design.objective: Use the Hurewicz map to read homotopy from homology.
mechanics: Hurewicz needle: send a sphere map to the homology class of its image.
If all lower groups vanish, the needle is an isomorphism in the first nonzero dimension.
design.math_check: The Hurewicz theorem: for (n−1)-connected X with n ≥ 2, πₙ(X) ≅ Hₙ(X); for n = 1, abelianization (Hatcher pp. 366–375).

levels.title: Hop Off
levels.concept: Fiber bundles and their long exact sequence; the Hopf fibration gives π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ.
levels.goal: Refute Null's World-3 claim: the Hopf map S³ → S² is essential.

design.site: The Hopf Ring — a floor encircled by a ring of interlinked glowing circles: every circle links every other.
design.story: Null's World 3 claim: every map S³ → S² is trivial. The Hopf Ring refutes it. The 3-sphere is a bundle of circles over the 2-sphere, every pair linked. Its long exact sequence shows π₃(S²) = ℤ, and the Hopf map is its generator.
design.objective: Refute Null's World 3 claim with the Hopf fibration.
mechanics: Fiber walk: each point of a small sphere island has a whole circle above it in the Ring; any two circles link.
Bundle sequence: the circle, the 3-sphere and the 2-sphere link into a long exact sequence of homotopy groups.
Since π₃(S¹) and π₂(S¹) vanish, π₃(S³) ≅ π₃(S²): the Hopf map counts as 1 — it is not trivial.
design.math_check: Fiber bundles, the long exact sequence of homotopy groups, the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S², π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ (Hatcher pp. 375–384). Refutes the World 3 claim.

levels.title: Stable Ground
levels.concept: Stable homotopy groups.

design.site: Stable Ground — a terrace far up the Spire where suspension no longer changes anything.
design.story: Suspend enough times and homotopy groups of spheres settle down: the stable stems. Gyroid charts the first few.
design.objective: Chart stable homotopy groups.

The first stems: ℤ, ℤ₂, ℤ₂, ℤ₂₄ — given by the book's table; the game shows them rather than computing all of them.

levels.title: Maps Are Classes
levels.concept: Cohomology as homotopy classes of maps to K(G, n).

design.site: The Classing Room — a room where readings (World 3) become maps into the One-Group Floors.
design.story: A cohomology class is the same as a map into a K(G, n) floor, up to sliding. Readings are maps.
design.objective: Turn readings into maps and back.
mechanics: Pull-back: map a place into K(G, n) and pull back the floor's fundamental reading.
Every reading arises this way, uniquely up to homotopy.
design.math_check: Hⁿ(X; G) ≅ ⟨X, K(G, n)⟩ for CW complexes (Hatcher pp. 393–405).

levels.title: Fibration Station
levels.concept: Fibrations and the homotopy lifting property.

design.site: Fibration Station — a station where every track lifts: the homotopy lifting property, for any path and any deformation.
design.story: Covers (World 1) lifted paths. Fibrations lift every deformation — and give long exact sequences. Any map can be turned into one.
design.objective: Lift deformations through fibrations and use their exact sequence.
mechanics: Lift: given a deformation below and a start above, the station builds the lift (homotopy lifting).
Path fibration: turn any map into a fibration by adding path tracks.
Loop space: the fiber of the path fibration is the loop space.
design.math_check: Fibrations, the homotopy lifting property, the long exact sequence, path-space fibrations and loop spaces (Hatcher pp. 405–410).

levels.title: A Twist in the Tower
levels.concept: Postnikov towers and k-invariants.

design.site: The Twist — a floor where the Spire's stages are joined by twisted brackets.
design.story: Every place is built as a tower of One-Group Floors joined by twists — the k-invariants. Null's final claim is that the twists don't matter. Here Gyroid sees that the same floors with different twists make different places.
design.objective: Build Postnikov towers and see that k-invariants change the space.
mechanics: Tower: stack stages Xₙ, each obtained from the one below with a K(πₙ, n) fiber.
Twist bracket: each stage is attached by a k-invariant (a cohomology class, 4-9).

Same groups, different twists: a two-stage tower with groups G (dimension m) and H (dimension n) is the product K(G,m) × K(H,n) when its k-invariant is zero, and a different, twisted place when it isn't.
design.math_check: Postnikov towers and k-invariants; spaces with the same homotopy groups can differ (Hatcher pp. 410–415).

levels.title: Obstruction Course
levels.concept: Obstruction theory: extend maps cell by cell; the obstruction is a cohomology class.

design.site: Obstruction Course — the last floor before the Crown: extend a map cell by cell, climbing as you go.
design.story: Extending a map over a cell-built place, one cell at a time: each step either succeeds or meets an obstruction — a cohomology class. The Extension Cord from World 0 (0-B) returns at full power.
design.objective: Extend maps cell by cell and read the obstructions.
mechanics: Climb: extend a map over the k-skeleton, then try each (k+1)-cell.
Obstruction: the map on a cell's boundary gives an element of πₖ; together they form a cohomology class.
Zero class: change the map on lower cells and continue.
design.math_check: Obstruction theory for extending maps; obstruction classes in Hᵏ⁺¹(X; πₖ(Y)) (Hatcher pp. 415–420).

structure.model: Super Mario Bros. 3: chapter = world, key concept = level, a castle closes each world, bonus levels hold additional topics.
structure.level_beats: Every level runs teach → practice → twist → master.
recurrence: Count Null's claim in each world exploits the blind spot of the invariant the player has so far; the next world's tool refutes it (see each world's null_claim).
Field guide: the same spaces (circle, disk, sphere, torus, Klein bottle, RP², figure-eight, Möbius band, later CPⁿ) recur, and each world fills in a new column of invariants for them.
Tools persist like power-ups; levels list `prerequisites` (must have) and `reuses` (actively re-tested).
Castles are cumulative tests of the levels they list.
